title: DAO (Data Access Object) Pattern
oneLiner: Encapsulates all interaction with a specific data source behind a clean API, so the rest of the app never touches raw queries directly.

hero.name: The Custodian
hero.catchphrase: I'm the only one who touches the raw data source. Everyone else asks me.
hero.power: Encapsulates every detail of talking to one specific data source (a database, a file, an external API) behind one clean, focused API.
hero.weakness: Because it's tied closely to a specific persistence mechanism, swapping that mechanism later usually means rewriting the DAO entirely, not just tweaking its internals.
hero.origin: The Custodian appeared after a report-generation module had raw JDBC connection-handling, SQL, and result-set parsing directly inside its business logic, tangled with formatting code.

story.problem: The report-generation module opens its own JDBC connection, writes raw SQL, and manually parses result sets — all directly inside a function that's also responsible for formatting the final report.
story.solution: The Custodian introduces a `ReportDAO` class that owns every detail of the connection, the query, and the result-set parsing. The report-generation code just calls `dao.getMonthlySales()` and gets back clean data.
story.result: Report-generation code no longer touches JDBC, SQL, or result sets at all. All of that lives inside ReportDAO, in one focused, well-tested place.

before: Raw data-source access is embedded directly in business logic
Connection handling and query logic are duplicated across features
Business logic is tightly coupled to one specific data-access mechanism
after: All data-source access is encapsulated in one DAO class
Connection handling and query logic exist in exactly one place
Business logic only depends on the DAO's clean method signatures

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A report-generation function has JDBC connection setup, raw SQL, and formatting logic all tangled in one 150-line method.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I need to add a new report, and I have to copy-paste this same JDBC connection and result-set parsing boilerplate again.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Custodian appears at the archive room's only entrance, the sole keeper of the raw data behind it.
panels.speaker: The Custodian
panels.dialogue: Stop reaching into the data source yourself. I'm the only one who touches raw queries — everyone else just asks me for what they need.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: ReportDAO.getMonthlySales() handles the connection, the query, and the parsing. Report-generation code just calls it.
panels.speaker: The Custodian
panels.dialogue: Report-generation code calls getMonthlySales() and gets clean data back. It never sees a connection, a query, or a result set.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The new report reuses ReportDAO's existing query methods, with zero copy-pasted boilerplate.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The new report reused existing DAO methods. Not one line of JDBC boilerplate was copy-pasted this time.

useWhen: You want a clear, single place responsible for all interaction with one specific data source.
Connection handling, query construction, and result parsing are currently duplicated across the codebase.
You want business logic to work with clean domain objects instead of raw rows, files, or API responses.
avoidWhen: The app already uses an ORM or Repository layer that provides this same encapsulation — adding a DAO on top would be redundant.
Data access is trivial enough (a single, simple query used in one place) that a dedicated class adds no real value.
You need persistence-mechanism independence — DAO is typically tied closely to one specific mechanism, unlike Repository's more abstracted, collection-like interface.
commonMistakes: Letting SQL, connection management, or result-parsing logic leak back out into business logic 'just this once', quietly defeating the encapsulation.

Confusing DAO with Repository — DAO is typically framed around one specific data source's raw access; Repository aims to feel like an in-memory collection regardless of source. The line blurs in practice, but the intent differs.
Not properly closing connections or handling errors inside the DAO, leaking resource-management bugs that were supposed to be contained there.
Building a DAO per table indiscriminately, even for tables that are always accessed together, instead of designing around actual business access patterns.
explanation.realWorldExample: Java EE's classic `UserDAO`/`OrderDAO` classes wrapping JDBC calls, and similar data-access classes wrapping file I/O or external API calls in other stacks, are textbook DAO implementations.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this actually different from Repository?

conversation.speaker: The Custodian
conversation.message: We overlap a lot in practice. I'm traditionally framed around ONE specific data source's raw access — a database, a file, an API. Repository leans harder into feeling like an in-memory COLLECTION, regardless of what's actually behind it.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Should I ever use both at once?

conversation.speaker: The Custodian
conversation.message: Some codebases do — a Repository built on top of one or more DAOs. In smaller apps, picking just one of us and being consistent about it matters far more than which name you use.

codeBattle.scenario: Your analytics module has JDBC connection setup and raw SQL query logic copy-pasted across four different report-generation functions, each handling connections and result parsing slightly differently.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Custodian centralizes all the raw connection handling, SQL, and result parsing into one class, so the four report functions call clean methods instead of duplicating JDBC boilerplate.

quiz.question: What does DAO encapsulate?
options: All interaction with a specific data source (connections, queries, result parsing) behind a clean API
A single algorithm that can be swapped at runtime
A notification system for multiple listeners
quiz.answer: All interaction with a specific data source (connections, queries, result parsing) behind a clean API
quiz.explanation: Encapsulating raw data-source access — and hiding it from the rest of the app — is DAO's core purpose.

quiz.question: What does business logic interact with once a DAO is in place?
options: Clean domain objects and method calls, never raw connections, queries, or result sets directly
Raw SQL strings passed as function arguments
A global variable holding the last query result
quiz.answer: Clean domain objects and method calls, never raw connections, queries, or result sets directly
quiz.explanation: The whole point is that business logic never sees the underlying data-access mechanism at all.

quiz.question: How does DAO typically differ from Repository, in intent?
options: DAO is traditionally framed around one specific data source's raw access; Repository aims to feel like an in-memory collection regardless of source
They are completely unrelated patterns with no overlap
Repository can only be used with files, DAO only with databases
DAO requires a NoSQL database; Repository requires SQL
quiz.answer: DAO is traditionally framed around one specific data source's raw access; Repository aims to feel like an in-memory collection regardless of source
quiz.explanation: The two patterns overlap heavily in practice, but this is the traditional distinction in intent between them.

quiz.question: What's a classic real-world example of DAO?
options: A Java EE `UserDAO` class wrapping JDBC calls behind clean methods
quiz.answer: A Java EE `UserDAO` class wrapping JDBC calls behind clean methods
quiz.explanation: This is the textbook, historically named example that gave the pattern its common name.
